title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: When Anna found Dolly home before her, she looked intently into her eyes, as if asking about the talk she had had with Vronsky, but in words she asked nothing.
"It must be dinnertime," she said. "We've not had any time to ourselves yet. I'm counting on the evening. Now I want to go and change. I expect you do too — we all got splashed at the building site."

Dolly went to her room and was amused by the situation. There was no way to change her dress; she had already put on her best one. But to mark her preparations for dinner somehow, she asked the maid to brush her dress, changed her cuffs and tie, and put some lace on her head.
"This is all I can manage," she said with a smile to Anna, who came in wearing yet a third dress, again of the utmost simplicity.

"Yes, we are too formal here," Anna said, as if apologizing for her magnificence. "Alexey is delighted at your visit — he rarely is at anything. He has completely lost his heart to you," she added. "You're not tired?"

There was no time to talk about anything before dinner. Going into the drawing room, they found Princess Varvara already there, and the gentlemen of the party in black frock coats. The architect wore a swallow-tail coat. Vronsky introduced the doctor and the steward to his guest; the architect he had already presented to her at the hospital.

A stout butler, resplendent with a smoothly shaven round chin and a starched white cravat, announced that dinner was ready, and the ladies got up. Vronsky asked Sviazhsky to take Anna Arkadyevna in, and offered his own arm to Dolly. Veslovsky beat Tushkevitch to it in offering his arm to Princess Varvara, so that Tushkevitch went in alone with the steward and the doctor.

The dinner, the dining room, the table service, the waiting at table, the wine, and the food were not only in keeping with the general tone of modern luxury throughout the house — they seemed even more sumptuous and modern. Darya Alexandrovna watched this luxury, which was new to her, and as a good housekeeper used to running a household — even though she never dreamed of adapting any of what she saw to her own household, since it was all in a style of luxury far beyond her own way of living — she could not help studying every detail and asking herself how and by whom it was all done. Vassenka Veslovsky, her husband, even Sviazhsky, and many other people she knew, would never have raised such a question, and would have happily accepted what every well-bred host tries to make his guests believe — that everything well-ordered in his house has cost him, the host, no trouble at all, but comes of itself. Darya Alexandrovna knew very well that even porridge for the children's breakfast does not come of itself, and that therefore, where so elaborate and grand a style of luxury was maintained, someone had to be giving it serious attention. And from the way Alexey Kirillovitch scanned the table, the way he nodded to the butler, and the way he offered Darya Alexandrovna her choice between cold and hot soup, she saw that it was all arranged and kept up by the care of the master of the house himself. It was obvious that it rested no more on Anna than on Veslovsky. She, Sviazhsky, the princess, and Veslovsky were equally guests, lightheartedly enjoying what had been laid on for them.

Anna was the hostess only in the matter of directing the conversation. And the conversation was a difficult one for the lady of the house at a small table with people present, such as the steward and the architect, from a completely different world, struggling not to be overawed by an elegance they were not used to, and unable to carry a large share of the general talk. But this difficult conversation Anna directed with her usual tact and naturalness, and indeed she did so with actual enjoyment, as Darya Alexandrovna noticed. The talk began with the row Tushkevitch and Veslovsky had taken alone together in the boat, and Tushkevitch began describing the latest boat races at the Petersburg Yacht Club. But Anna, seizing the first pause, turned to the architect at once, to draw him out of his silence.

"Nikolay Ivanitch was struck," she said, meaning Sviazhsky, "at how the new building has progressed since the last time he was here; but I'm there every day, and every day I am amazed at how quickly it goes up."

"It's first-rate working for his excellency," said the architect with a smile (he was respectful and self-possessed, with a quiet sense of his own dignity). "It's a very different matter from dealing with district authorities. Where you would have to fill out reams of paper, here I just call on the count, and we settle the business in three words."
"The American way of doing business," Sviazhsky said with a smile.
"Yes, over there they build sensibly...."
The conversation turned to the misuse of political power in the United States, but Anna quickly steered it onto another subject, so as to draw the steward into the talk.
"Have you ever seen a reaping machine?" she said to Darya Alexandrovna. "We had just ridden over to look at one when we ran into you. It was the first time I had ever seen one."
"How do they work?" Dolly asked.
"Exactly like little scissors. A plank, and a row of little scissors. Like this."

Anna took up a knife and fork in her beautiful white, ring-covered hands and began demonstrating how the machine worked. It was clear that she saw nothing would be made clear by her demonstration; but, aware that her talk was pleasing and her hands beautiful, she kept on explaining.
"More like little penknives," Veslovsky said playfully, his eyes never leaving her.
Anna gave a barely perceptible smile but made no reply. "Isn't it true, Karl Fedoritch — it's just like little scissors?" she said to the steward.
"_Oh, ja_," the German answered. _"Es ist ein ganz einfaches Ding,"_ and he began to explain the way the machine was built.
"It's a shame it doesn't bind too. I saw one at the Vienna exhibition that binds with wire," said Sviazhsky. "Those would be more profitable to use."

_"Es kommt drauf an.... Der Preis vom Draht muss ausgerechnet werden."_ And the German, his silence broken, turned to Vronsky. _"Das lässt sich ausrechnen, Erlaucht."_ The German was already feeling in the pocket where he kept his pencil and the notebook he always wrote in, but, remembering that he was at a dinner table and noticing Vronsky's chilly glance, he checked himself. _"Zu compliziert, macht zu viel Klopot,"_ he concluded.
_"Wünscht man Dochots, so hat man auch Klopots,"_ said Vassenka Veslovsky, mimicking the German. _"J'adore l'allemand,"_ he added, turning to Anna again with the same smile.
_"Cessez,"_ she said, with playful severity.
"We expected to find you in the fields, Vassily Semyonitch," she said to the doctor, a sickly-looking man. "Did you go?"
"I went, but I took flight," the doctor answered with grim jocularity.
"So you got a good walk?"
"Splendid!"
"And how was the old woman? I hope it's not typhus?"
"Typhus, no — but it is taking a bad turn."
"What a pity!" said Anna, and, having paid the dues of civility to her own circle, she turned back to her own friends.
"It would still be a hard task to build a machine from your description, Anna Arkadyevna," Sviazhsky said jokingly.

"Oh, no — why?" said Anna, with a smile that betrayed she knew there was something charming in her disquisition on the machine, something Sviazhsky had noticed. This new touch of girlish coquettishness made an unpleasant impression on Dolly.
"But Anna Arkadyevna's grasp of architecture is marvelous," said Tushkevitch.
"Indeed, I heard Anna Arkadyevna yesterday talking about plinths and damp-courses," said Veslovsky. "Have I got the words right?"
"It's hardly marvelous when you live around it and hear about it constantly," said Anna. "Though I'll bet you don't even know what houses are built out of?"
Darya Alexandrovna could see that Anna disliked the tone of teasing that ran between herself and Veslovsky, and yet kept slipping into it in spite of herself.
Vronsky's behavior in this matter was completely unlike Levin's. He clearly attached no importance to Veslovsky's chatter; on the contrary, he encouraged his jokes.
"Come now, Veslovsky, tell us — how are the stones held together?"
"By cement, of course."
"Bravo! And what is cement?"
"Oh, some sort of paste... no, putty," said Veslovsky, raising a general laugh.

The company at dinner, with the exception of the doctor, the architect, and the steward, who stayed locked in gloomy silence, kept up a conversation that never paused, glancing off one subject and fastening on another, and now and then stinging one or another to the quick. At one point Darya Alexandrovna felt cut to the quick herself, and grew so hot that she actually flushed, and afterwards wondered whether she had said anything too sharp or out of turn. Sviazhsky started talking about Levin, describing his odd view that machinery was simply harmful in its effect on Russian agriculture.

"I have not the pleasure of knowing this Monsieur Levin," Vronsky said, smiling, "but most likely he has never seen the machines he condemns; or if he has seen and tried any, he must have done so in some odd way, with some Russian imitation, not a real machine from abroad. What sort of view can anyone have on such a subject?"
"Turkish views, generally speaking," Veslovsky said, turning to Anna with a smile.

"I can't defend his opinions," Darya Alexandrovna said, firing up. "But I can say that he is a highly cultivated man, and if he were here, he would know very well how to answer you, though I am not capable of doing so."

"I like him very much, and we are great friends," Sviazhsky said, smiling good-naturedly. "_Mais pardon, il est un petit peu toqué_; he maintains, for example, that the district councils and the arbitration boards are all of no use, and he refuses to take any part in any of it."

"It is our Russian apathy," Vronsky said, pouring water from an iced decanter into a fine glass on a high stem. "We've no sense of the duties our privileges impose on us, and so we refuse to recognize those duties."
"I know no man more conscientious in the discharge of his duties," Darya Alexandrovna said, irritated by Vronsky's tone of superiority.

"As for me," Vronsky went on, evidently for some reason keenly stirred by this conversation, "such as I am, on the contrary, I am extremely grateful for the honor they have done me — thanks to Nikolay Ivanitch" (he indicated Sviazhsky) — "in electing me a justice of the peace. I consider that, for me, the duty of being present at the session, of judging some peasants' quarrel about a horse, is as important as anything else I can do. And I shall regard it as an honor if they elect me to the district council. It is only in that way that I can pay back what I enjoy as a landowner. Unfortunately people do not understand the weight that the great landowners ought to carry in the state."

It was strange to Darya Alexandrovna to hear how serenely certain he was of being right at his own table. She thought of how Levin, who held the opposite view, was just as positive in his opinions at his own table. But she loved Levin, and so she was on his side.

"So can we count on you for the coming elections, count?" said Sviazhsky. "But you must come down a little early, so as to be on the spot by the eighth. If you would do me the honor of staying with me."

"I rather agree with your _beau-frère_," said Anna, "though not quite on his grounds," she added, smiling. "I'm afraid we have too many of these public duties nowadays. Just as in the old days there were so many government officials that you had to call in an official for every little thing, so now everybody is doing some sort of public service. Alexey has been here six months, and I believe he is already a member of five or six different bodies. _Du train que cela va_, the whole of life will go on it. And I am afraid that with such a multiplication of these bodies, they'll all end up as mere form. How many are you a member of, Nikolay Ivanitch?" she turned to Sviazhsky. "Over twenty, I think."

Anna spoke lightly, but irritation could be heard in her tone. Darya Alexandrovna, watching Anna and Vronsky closely, caught it at once. She noticed too that as Anna spoke, Vronsky's face had immediately taken on a serious, stubborn look. Noticing that, and Princess Varvara hurrying in to change the subject by talking of Petersburg acquaintances, and remembering what Vronsky had said, apparently out of nowhere, in the garden, about his work in the country, Dolly guessed that this question of public activity was tied to some deep private disagreement between Anna and Vronsky.

The dinner, the wine, the table decoration were all very good; but it was all like what Darya Alexandrovna had seen at formal dinners and balls — which in recent years had become quite unfamiliar to her — it all had the same impersonal, constrained character, and so, on an ordinary day in a small circle of friends, it made an unpleasant impression on her.

After dinner they sat on the terrace for a while, then went on to play lawn tennis. The players, split into two parties, took up positions on either side of a tightly drawn net with gilt poles on the carefully leveled and rolled croquet ground. Darya Alexandrovna tried to play, but it took her a long time to grasp the game, and by the time she did, she was so tired that she sat down beside Princess Varvara and simply watched the rest. Her partner, Tushkevitch, gave up too, but the others kept the game going for a long time. Sviazhsky and Vronsky both played very well and seriously. They kept a sharp eye on the balls served to them, and without hurrying or getting in each other's way, they ran up to them deftly, waited for the bounce, and returned them cleanly and accurately over the net. Veslovsky played worse than the others. He was too eager, but he kept the players lively with his high spirits. His laughter and shouting never stopped. Like the other men of the party, with the ladies' permission, he took off his coat, and his solid, handsome figure in his white shirtsleeves, with his red sweating face and his impulsive movements, made a picture that printed itself vividly on the memory.
When Darya Alexandrovna lay in bed that night, as soon as she shut her eyes, she saw Vassenka Veslovsky flying about the croquet ground.

During the game Darya Alexandrovna had not been enjoying herself. She did not like the light, bantering tone that was kept up the whole time between Vassenka Veslovsky and Anna, and the general unnaturalness of grown-ups, all alone without children, playing a children's game. But, to avoid breaking up the party and to fill the time somehow, she joined the game again after a rest and pretended to be enjoying it. All that day it felt to her as though she were acting in a play with actors cleverer than she was, and that her bad acting was spoiling the whole performance. She had come intending to stay two days, if all went well. But that evening, during the game, she made up her mind to go home the next day. The maternal cares and worries she had so hated on the way out now, after a day without them, struck her in a quite different light, and drew her back to them.

When, after evening tea and a row on the river by night, Darya Alexandrovna went alone to her room, took off her dress, and began arranging her thin hair for the night, she felt a great sense of relief.
It was positively unpleasant to her to think that Anna was about to come in to see her. She longed to be alone with her own thoughts.
